# Designing the Future of Work — A Framework for Global Adoption

**Prepared for discussion by the Executive Committee, with People, Real Estate/Workplace, IT, Legal & Tax, and the regional Managing Directors in attendance.**

*Circulated for comment before any decision is sought. Figures marked "illustrative" are placeholders to be replaced once the discovery work in §12 reports. The principles, the allocation of discretion, and the decision requests in §14 are not placeholders — they are put forward for approval.*

---

## 0. Executive summary

**The situation, stated plainly.** We are being asked to settle a question that is usually framed as *"how many days in the office?"* — and that framing is, we would gently suggest, the reason so many companies have now announced three positions in four years. Attendance is an input. It is also the only input that is easy to count, which is why it tends to become the policy by default.

**The premise we would propose instead.** Location and schedule are not benefits to be granted or withdrawn. They are design variables in a production system, in exactly the way that layout, batch size and queue discipline are on a factory floor. The question is not *how much freedom can we tolerate*, but *what configuration of place, time and tooling gets the work done well, for whom, and at what cost to whom*.

**The organising idea, in one line:**

> **A thin global frame, a thick local fill — with the burden of justification resting on the restriction, and the burden of clarity resting on whoever holds the discretion.**

Very few things need to be true everywhere. A great deal needs to be decided close to the work. But — and this is the point most easily missed in a company headquartered in a low-context, individualist culture — **discretion that is merely permitted is not the same as discretion that is supplied.** In several of our largest markets, an employee will not act on a freedom that has not been visibly and specifically sanctioned by their manager. A framework that says only *"you decide"* will be read as generous in Amsterdam and as an abdication in Tokyo, Seoul, Mumbai and much of the Gulf.

**What we would ask colleagues to consider committing to:**

| | Commitment | Earned by | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage 1** | Eight global invariants (§3) published, plus a mandatory **team charter** for every team of ≥4 | Discovery findings; regional legal review; works council consultation | Month 4 |
| **Stage 2** | Six contrasting pilot sites operating under the frame, with published results including the unflattering ones | Pilot instrumentation and honest reporting | Month 10 |
| **Stage 3** | Portfolio, tooling and reward decisions taken *on the evidence*, not ahead of it | Stage 2 evidence; lease expiry calendar | Month 12–24 |

**Illustrative investment ask (order of magnitude; to be firmed at Month 4):**

| Item | Year-1 cost | Note |
|---|---:|---|
| Discovery: instrumented listening in 12–15 countries, local-language facilitation, third-party interviewers | £0.6–0.9M | Non-negotiable prerequisite; see §12 |
| Common collaboration stack consolidation, decision-log and search layer | £1.5–3.0M | Consolidation should be broadly self-funding by Year 2 |
| Accessibility, bandwidth-floor and translation/transcription capability | £0.4–0.8M | The single highest-leverage equity spend, in our view |
| Workplace re-purposing (pilot sites only) | £2.0–4.0M | Deliberately *not* a portfolio-wide programme yet |
| Manager capability: outcome contracting, distributed team leadership | £1.0–1.8M | ~4,000 people managers, blended delivery |
| Home/remote work allowance harmonisation | Country-by-country | Legally mandated in several jurisdictions; not discretionary |
| Programme cell (5–6 people, deliberately small) | £0.9M/yr | See §11 on why small |
| **Total (Year 1, indicative)** | **£6.4–11.2M** | Against illustrative Year-2+ portfolio and attrition offsets of £15–30M/yr |

**Illustrative return.** On assumptions to be validated in discovery: portfolio efficiency of 20–35% of controllable occupancy cost as leases roll; a reduction in regretted attrition among high-performers of 2–4 points; access to talent markets currently closed to us; and a meeting-load reduction that is real money but that we would not attempt to monetise in front of this audience. *If discovery does not support the portfolio or retention figures, the correct recommendation is to adopt the near-zero-cost principles, decline the capital, and revisit in twelve months.*

**Decisions requested (also §14):** appoint a sponsor and a single accountable owner (Week 0); authorise discovery and works council consultation (Week 0); approve the eight invariants and the team charter mechanism (Month 4); approve pilot funding (Month 4); take portfolio and reward decisions only at Month 12+ (§10, §13).

---

## 1. How we would suggest this is taken forward

A framework of this kind does not succeed by being announced. Before anything is published company-wide, we would propose:

1. **Separate one-to-one conversations with each regional Managing Director**, in advance of any collective session, so each has the opportunity to shape the parts touching their markets before they are asked to endorse them in a room. Objections raised privately can be accommodated; objections raised publicly become positions.
2. **A short, sponsor-signed statement on the last two years** — that the reversals were failures of framing under uncertainty, not of anyone's judgement, and that **nobody's standing will be affected by having advocated a position that the evidence has since moved past.** This costs nothing and, in our view, is the precondition for candour rather than compliance.
3. **A published statement of what is *not* on the table**, settled in advance. Colleagues become markedly more inventive once they are confident the floor is solid:
   - safety, and physical presence where the work is physically bound;
   - regulatory, export-control and client-confidentiality obligations;
   - contractual customer commitments;
   - local employment law and collective agreements;
   - information security and data residency.
4. **Publication of every discovery finding**, including those unflattering to the sponsor, to the executive's own working preferences, and to headquarters. Particularly those.
5. **Deliberate design for indirect feedback.** In a good number of our markets, we will not be told what is wrong; we will be told that everything is fine, and then attrition will tell us later. Anonymous instrumentation, third-party interviewers, local-language facilitators and observed behaviour (§13) are not luxuries here — they are the only reliable channel.

The tone throughout should be that every regional practice we currently find odd is a rational response to conditions we have not yet troubled to understand. Those conditions are the thing to design around.

---

## 2. What we are actually deciding

It may help to separate four questions that are routinely collapsed into one, and to note that they belong to different owners and different timescales.

| Question | Really about | Decided by | Timescale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Where** does work happen? | Place: home, office, third space, customer site, plant | Team charter, within the frame | Continuous |
| **When** does work happen? | Time: overlap, asynchrony, predictability | Team charter, within the frame | Continuous |
| **How** does work move? | Tooling, written record, decision rights | Global — genuinely | Months |
| **What is it worth?** | Pay, reward, career, status | Global policy, local law | 12–24 months |

Most of the corporate world's difficulty, we suspect, comes from answering the first question globally and the third question locally. We would propose the reverse.

---

## 3. The eight invariants — the thin global frame

These we would suggest apply everywhere, without local variation, and are the *only* things that do. Each carries an expiry date (§11).

**1. Design for the work, not for the room.**
Presence is required when the work requires it, and is otherwise a matter for the team. No global attendance quota. Quotas are a proxy for a diagnosis nobody has done.

**2. Distance is not the problem; asymmetry is.**
The failure mode of hybrid is not remoteness but a *two-tier meeting*: some in the room with the whiteboard and the corridor afterwards, some on a screen at the far end of the table. Therefore: for any gathering with at least one remote participant, **the meeting runs in the remote-inclusive format** — one person, one screen, one channel, or a properly equipped room with an accountable facilitator. This is a hard rule because it is the one everyone privately intends to break.

**3. Written by default; synchronous by exception, and earned.**
A global company that runs on meetings is a company that runs on whoever lives nearest headquarters. Decisions, rationale and dissent are recorded in a searchable place. A meeting is justified when the work is generative, relational, or contested — not when it is informational.

**4. A thin global frame, a thick local fill — subsidiarity as the default.**
Decisions sit at the lowest level that can see the whole of the work. **The burden of justification lies with the restriction, not with the freedom.** Anyone imposing a constraint above team level should be able to state, in writing, what breaks without it.

**5. Flexibility must be supplied, not merely permitted.**
Because permission is not culturally portable. Every manager states, explicitly and specifically, what their people may decide for themselves. "Use your judgement" is not a policy in most of the world; it is a test people are afraid to fail.

**6. Proximity must not pay.**
Promotion, pay progression, high-visibility assignment and access to sponsorship are monitored by working pattern and by location relative to leadership. Divergence is treated as a defect in the system, not a difference in the people. (§10)

**7. Nobody permanently absorbs the inconvenience of geography.**
Overlap windows are declared, recurring "awkward hour" meetings rotate across regions, and no region is structurally assigned the night shift for the convenience of another. Where rotation is impossible, the burden is explicitly compensated.

**8. Flexibility is redefined, not withdrawn, for location-bound work.**
Roughly [illustrative: 45–55%] of our people cannot choose where they work. For them, the currency is **time**: schedule predictability, shift-swap agency, advance rostering notice, and genuine choice within it. A framework that delivers freedom to knowledge workers and nothing to the plant, the lab, the field and the service centre would be worse than no framework at all — and would be read, correctly, as a statement about whose work we value.

---

## 4. Work archetypes — the analytical layer beneath the frame

Rather than classify *people* (by seniority, by role title, by "remote-eligible"), we would suggest classifying *work*. Most people do several of these in a week; the mix determines the pattern.

| Archetype | Characteristics | Place implication | Time implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Concentrated** | Individual, low interdependence, high cognitive load | Location-indifferent; home often superior | Fully asynchronous |
| **Coordinated production** | Interdependent, procedural, hand-off driven | Location-indifferent if instrumented | Async with a declared overlap window |
| **Generative** | Divergent, ambiguous, conflict-prone, trust-consuming | Periodic co-presence has genuine, measurable value | Intensive blocks, not weekly drip |
| **Relational** | Building trust with new colleagues, clients, partners | Co-presence, especially at the start of a relationship | Episodic, planned well ahead |
| **Apprenticeship** | Early-career, tacit-knowledge transfer, learning by overhearing | Proximity-dependent; the most under-priced item in every remote debate | Sustained, not episodic |
| **Response** | Incident, crisis, escalation | Location-indifferent; overlap-dependent | Follow-the-sun coverage |
| **Bound** | Plant, lab, hardware, clinical, retail, customer site | Fixed | Shift and roster design (Invariant 8) |

**The uncomfortable implication we would rather name early.** Concentrated and coordinated work argues for distribution. Apprenticeship and relational work argue for co-presence. Those two truths are both real, and they fall unevenly by age and tenure. A framework that optimises purely for the preferences of experienced staff will quietly disadvantage the people who have least voice in the consultation. We would suggest the early-career cohort is designed for *first*, deliberately, and that the design is a stated obligation of senior staff rather than a facility offered to juniors.

---

## 5. The local fill — how variation is handled without incoherence

Four layers, with explicit ownership. Anything not reserved to a higher layer belongs to the lower one.

| Layer | Owns | Constrained by |
|---|---|---|
| **Global** | The eight invariants; the common tool stack; pay architecture; the definitions used for measurement | Board |
| **Country / cluster** | Legal compliance, works council agreements, allowances, tax and PE guardrails, public-holiday and observance calendars, infrastructure floors | The invariants |
| **Team charter** | Anchor days, overlap window, response-time expectations, meeting norms, where and when co-presence is required, how decisions are recorded | The two layers above |
| **Individual** | Everything else, including how hours are arranged within the charter | The charter |

### 5.1 The team charter

We would propose this is the real instrument of the whole framework — one page, written by the team, signed by the manager, published where any colleague can read it, and reviewed twice a year. Seven questions:

1. What work do we do that genuinely benefits from being in the same room, and how often is that actually true?
2What is our declared overlap window, in every member's local time, and who absorbed the inconvenience of setting it?
3. What is our expected response time — and, more importantly, what is *not* expected? (When is nobody obliged to reply?)
4. Where do decisions get recorded, such that a colleague on the other side of the world can reconstruct the reasoning without asking anyone?
